analysis.one_liner: Lets states take over energy leasing and permitting on federal land without federal environmental review.
analysis.headline: The bill sat in the Senate Energy Committee for two years without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor, and expired when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would let any state take over leasing, permitting, and regulating oil, gas, and other energy development on federal land inside its borders just by filing a declaration with three federal departments [S2][S3]. Once a state took over, its decisions would be exempt from the National Environmental Policy Act, the Endangered Species Act, the National Historic Preservation Act, and the Administrative Procedure Act — meaning no environmental review, no endangered-species checks, and no ability to challenge decisions in court [S2][S3]. Royalties would still be collected at federal levels and deposited in federal accounts, but states could keep the fees they charge applicants [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Energy companies — chiefly oil, gas, and mining firms — that want to develop federal land would gain the most: state-level permitting is typically faster than federal permitting, and the bill removes environmental review, endangered-species consultation, historic-preservation checks, and the right to sue over those decisions [S2][S3]. States with large energy industries would also gain control over development decisions on federal land within their borders and could keep the application fees they collect [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Energy companies drilling on federal land

how_it_helps.text: Any state could take over leasing, permitting, and regulation of oil, natural gas, and other energy development on federal land simply by submitting a declaration that it has its own regulatory program — no federal approval or study required [S2][S3].

State actions replacing federal ones would be exempt from the National Environmental Policy Act, the Endangered Species Act, the National Historic Preservation Act, and the Administrative Procedure Act, so development could proceed without environmental review or court challenges [S2][S3].
States could collect and keep processing fees from lease and permit applicants, giving them a revenue stream for administering the program [S3].

The bill preserved federal royalty levels — state-issued leases had to collect the same royalties the federal government would have — which supporters offered as assurance that taxpayers would not lose revenue [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The American public, which collectively owns federal land, would bear the cost: development decisions on shared public land could be made by a single state with no environmental review, no protection for endangered species outside excluded areas, and no administrative process or judicial review for citizens to challenge a lease or permit [S2][S3]. The bill excludes tribal trust land, national parks, wildlife refuges, and designated wilderness as of 2013, but all other federal land — including forests and land managed by the Bureau of Land Management — would be open to state-controlled development [S2][S3]. States would take on administrative costs, offset by the fees they could charge applicants [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Everyone who owns or uses public land

drawbacks.text: By exempting state actions from the National Environmental Policy Act and the Endangered Species Act, the bill would eliminate environmental review and endangered-species safeguards for development on land owned by all Americans, and by exempting it from the Administrative Procedure Act it would strip citizens of the ability to challenge those decisions in court [S2][S3].

The bill applies to all federal land except tribal trust land, national parks, wildlife refuges, and congressionally designated wilderness as of May 2013 — leaving national forests, Bureau of Land Management land, and land protected after 2013 subject to state-controlled development [S2][S3].

A good-faith case for the bill exists: federal permitting on federal land can take years, states already regulate drilling on their own land, and the bill kept federal royalty levels intact so public revenue would not drop — but those assurances do not restore the removed environmental review or legal recourse [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits would flow narrowly and quickly to energy developers in the form of faster, harder-to-challenge permits. The costs would be broad and lasting: no environmental review, no endangered-species consultation, and no judicial check on development of land the public owns. Even the revenue-protection feature only preserved the status quo on royalties; it did not compensate for the loss of the legal processes that let citizens weigh in on how shared land is used. On balance, the bill traded durable public protections for industry convenience.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Markwayne Mullin introduced the bill on January 23, 2023; it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources [S1][S5].
No senator cosponsored the bill at any point [S4].

The Energy and Natural Resources Committee never held a hearing, marked it up, or reported it out, and the full Senate never voted on it; the bill expired when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary citizens who own and use federal land came out ahead, because the federal environmental review, endangered-species protections, and right to challenge development decisions all remain in place. Energy companies hoping for faster state-run permitting on federal land gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Public-land users; energy developers gained nothing

for.name: Sen. Markwayne Mullin
for.role: U.S. Senator from Oklahoma; bill's sole sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Energy and Natural Resources Committee; recruited no cosponsors

against.name: Sen. Joe Manchin
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it in committee until the Congress expired

against.name: 49 of 49 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: None joined as cosponsors; only the sponsor signed on

sides.party_line_note: The bill never came to a vote; not a single senator besides its Republican sponsor cosponsored it, so no partisan breakdown exists beyond one name.

industries.note: The bill would have let states issue federal-land drilling leases and permits without environmental review, endangered-species consultation, or the risk of court challenge — a direct win for companies seeking faster access to federal land. It died, so their federal-land permitting rules stay as they were.

The bill covered 'other forms of energy' and mineral development on federal land, not just oil and gas, so geothermal, renewable, and mining developers would have gotten the same fast-track, no-review path. It never advanced.

States could have taken control of federal-land energy decisions and kept the application fees they charged, gaining authority and revenue. Their citizens, however, would share the loss of environmental review on public land.
